title: The Surprisingly Similar Troubles with Strategies Based on Coercion or Engagement gagement
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a despairing email from a 27-year veteran teacher named Jennifer, whose students were not returning work or showing up to virtual class despite vague threats about being 'held responsible,' Dave Stuart Jr. argues that both of education's two dominant motivational strategies — coercion and engagement — share a deeper flaw: they treat students as objects to be managed rather than as persons. Drawing on early-twentieth-century educational philosopher Charlotte Mason's claim that 'children are born persons,' he argues that coercive systems built on carrots and sticks are dehumanizing and unsustainable, especially once students sense that the threatened consequences ('failing' in a pandemic year) carry no real weight. He then turns the same critique on engagement-centered pedagogy, arguing that the concept has become a fuzzy buzzword whose classroom applications often devolve into knowledge-lite tech gimmicks that widen equity gaps and that, at root, engagement-chasing is just another way of working around a student's will rather than partnering with it. His proposed alternative combines a knowledge-rich, 'generous curriculum' in the Charlotte Mason tradition with deliberate cultivation of the five key beliefs (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy) that he argues actually drive durable student motivation, whether instruction happens in person or remotely.
points: Coercive systems built on vague threats of being 'held responsible' or a student 'failing' tend to increase pressure without improving motivation, especially once students sense the consequences carry no real weight.

Both coercion-based and engagement-based motivational strategies share a common flaw: they treat the student as an object to be managed or a brain to be stimulated rather than, per Charlotte Mason, a 'person' with agency, intellect, emotion, and will.

Engagement-centered professional development often devolves into knowledge-lite tech gimmicks and novel projects that advantage students who already have knowledge-rich experiences outside school, worsening rather than closing equity gaps.

Stuart's proposed alternative pairs a knowledge-rich 'generous curriculum' with deliberate cultivation of the five key beliefs underlying motivation, arguing this humanizes learning whether it happens in person or remotely.
quotes: I'm stuck in my home three days a week teaching remotely. Two days a week I teach remotely from my packed up classroom. I've been at this gig for nearly 27 years, so retirement is an option. I mentioned to someone that I'd rather hand out stickers at Walmart.
I know that vague threats of repercussion tend to increase pressure without improving motivation or performance.

Charlotte Mason, an educational philosopher who founded schools in the first decades of the twentieth century, wrote in 1922 that "children are born persons," and from this naturally follows the idea that such personhood "must not be encroached upon… by the direct use of fear" but rather that children "should have a generous curriculum.
Systems that have long relied on procuring student motivation via carrots and sticks are dehumanizing: to teachers, to students, to families.
Almost always, this talk of engagement is painfully fuzzy. It's been buzzwordified — and I mean that practically, not cynically.

Such professional development often devolves into knowledge-lite explorations of cool tech and novel projects, and such knowledge-liteness always advantages those who are privileged to experience knowledge-rich contexts outside of school.
Designing engaging lessons is ultimately about figuring out a way past the will rather than thinking deeply about what it means for an education to seek a partnership with the will.
